stem: A rectangular prism has a surface area of {=s} cm$^2$ and a volume of {=v} cm$^3$. Its length, breadth and height are all multiplied by the same constant factor, and the volume of the new prism is {=n} cm$^3$. Calculate the surface area of the new prism, in cm$^2$.
solution: Let each of the length, breadth and height be multiplied by a constant factor of $k$, so the new dimensions are $kl$, $kb$ and $kh$.
The new volume is $V_{\text{new}}=(kl)\times(kb)\times(kh)=k^3\times l\times b\times h=k^3V$.
The surface area of a rectangular prism is $S=2(lb+lh+bh)$, so $S_{\text{new}}=2(kl\times kb+kl\times kh+kb\times kh)=k^2\times2(lb+lh+bh)=k^2S$.
So the surface area is multiplied by a factor of $k^2={=k}^2={=k*k}$.
notes: Advanced: links the two factors of this objective. Book Ex 13.6 Q4b gives the all-three-dimensions case (V_new = k^3 V); here the student must run it backwards (k^3 = V_new / V, so k, a perfect cube 8, 27 or 64) and then carry k into the surface area (S_new = k^2 S, from S = 2(lb + lh + bh)). The inverse step is an extension of the book's method, not a new technique: same substitution kl, kb, kh, only the unknown has moved. The numbers are consistent by construction: l, b, h are drawn first and the stated surface area and volume are computed from them, so no impossible prism is ever shown (the student never needs l, b, h themselves). Worked check: l=2, b=3, h=4, k=2 gives S=52, V=24, new volume 192, k^3=8, k=2, new surface area 4 x 52 = 208, which equals the direct computation with sides 4, 6, 8: 2(24+32+48)=208. Largest values: new volume 8000, new surface area under 1700. Whole-number answers always, since k is an integer and S is an integer.
